WHY I DON’T BET EVERYTHING ON AI 🤖

The market has been wobbly lately, and the AI trade has taken the biggest hit. The chip index $SOXX is down around 13% in October. Last Thursday, it fell almost 7%, as worries about debt in the data center build-out spread.

My portfolio has held up well through this.

It is down about 2,8% in October. That is not a month I celebrate, but for a portfolio that still has a large share in AI infrastructure, it is a much smaller hit than many AI-focused investors are taking. On that Thursday, when chip stocks fell almost 7%, the four main health care stocks in the portfolio rose 1,99%.

There is a reason for this.

Last year, I put serious work into building 𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝗹𝗴𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗺 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗽𝘀 𝗺𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗺𝘆 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘆. It looks at how my stocks move together, and especially at how they behave on the worst days. Its job is to make sure nothing in my portfolio depends on the same story.

I am still bullish on AI infrastructure. Demand for compute is very strong, GPU rental prices are at their highest level this year, and companies like $ANT.24-7  are growing revenue at a pace we rarely see. About a quarter of my portfolio is in AI hardware and infrastructure, such as $MU, TSMC, and AMD.

The rest is spread across very different parts of the economy: Healthcare, energy, banks and insurance, European defense, industrials, and consumer staples.

Healthcare is a good example. Around 17% of the portfolio is now in $JNJ, $LLY, Merck, and Bristol-Myers Squibb, and I bought the first of these positions back in July. Their growth is driven by something completely different from the AI trade:

The world’s population is getting older. According to the WHO, 1 in 6 people will be 60 or older by 2030, and by 2050 that group will have doubled to 2,1 billion people. Older people need more medicine and more treatment, whether or not a neocloud can refinance its debt.

You can see this in the numbers.

Over the past year, there were 36 trading days where the chip index fell more than 3%. On those days, 𝗺𝘆 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗹𝘁𝗵𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗰𝗸𝘀 𝗿𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝟬.𝟵% 𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗲. In other words, they tended to go up on the days when the AI trade was at its worst. This pattern isn't guaranteed to continue, but it is the kind of protection I was looking for. 

Finding stocks like these is exactly what the algorithm was built for.

Diversification has a price, and I want to be clear about it. When the AI trade runs hard, a portfolio like mine could lag for a period compared to a portfolio that is 100% AI-focused, but I accept that trade-off. 

My portfolio will not overperform every day, every week, or every month. However, I want to make it more likely to overperform over a longer stretch, and I believe this is the best way to do it.

The main reason this approach makes sense is that big losses are expensive: a 30% loss requires a 43% gain to get back to where you started. And 𝗯𝗶𝗴 𝗹𝗼𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗹𝗶𝗸𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝗶𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗴𝗼 𝗮𝗹𝗹-𝗶𝗻 𝗼𝗻 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺𝗲. My goal is to compound steadily over many years, not to win every single month.

I still monitor the credit stress closely, and I will act if something breaks. But I don’t need to make big, sudden moves when the market gets nervous, because I spread the risk months before the nervousness started.

Thanks for copying and following 🙏
